title: Busy seasons
hookLine: new babies, deadlines, moves: shrink, don't stop, like Brother Lawrence turning the cake in the pan for love of God
tomorrow: too sick to move, a woman in bed saw visions. what did they say?

lines: A MONK WHO DISLIKED THE KITCHEN.
cards: Pans clanging. Someone shouting an order. A sink full of dishes.
That was Brother Lawrence's workplace. He was a lay brother in a Carmelite monastery in Paris, put to work in the kitchen, and he admitted he had a natural dislike for the job.
Yet he told a visitor that, for him, the busy time in the kitchen, with several people calling for different things at once, was no different from the time of prayer.

teach.h: SHRINK PRAYER TO FIT THE WORK.
teach.b: How? Not by finding extra hours. By shrinking prayer until it fit inside the work.

teach.h: THE PRACTICE OF THE PRESENCE OF GOD.
teach.b: His way has a name, and it became the title of the little book made from his talks and letters: The Practice of the Presence of God.
Instead of waiting for a quiet hour, he turned to God with a word or a glance, again and again, in the middle of things. We can do little things for God, he said.

teach.h: TURNING THE CAKE FOR LOVE OF GOD.
teach.b: He would turn the cake frying in the pan for love of God. A sizzle, a flip, a moment of attention, offered. He still kept the set times of prayer his order asked of him.

teach.h: NO TIME COUNTS AS TIME AWAY.
teach.b: He just refused to let the loud hours count as time away. That's the teaching his tradition passed on: in a busy season, prayer doesn't stop.
It gets smaller, and it moves into the work. For a rule in a season of a new baby, a deadline or a move, Lawrence's way isn't to drop the practice until things calm down.
It's to shrink it to something you can hold in one hand. A breath at the stove. One word at the sink.
A small thing, done for love, in the middle of the noise.

how: Christians still read Brother Lawrence's The Practice of the Presence of God and try his way of turning to God briefly in the middle of work. On a personal rule, a busy-season version is a shrunken practice that fits a full day.

the months when a company makes most of its money
stretches too full for your usual practice, so it shrinks

s: Brother Lawrence loved kitchen work from the start
he admitted a natural dislike for it, and prayed in it anyway.
Lawrence kept his set prayer times too
he prayed at the set times his superiors directed; he just refused to count the busy hours as time away.
in a busy season, the wise move is to pause practice until life calms down
Lawrence's way is to shrink it into the work, not stop it.

games.q: your sister has a newborn and says she's 'given up' praying until the baby sleeps through the night. what would Brother Lawrence suggest?
o: a word or a glance toward God in the middle of the feeding and rocking.
wait for the quiet months; prayer needs a calm, set-apart hour.
wake up an hour earlier than the baby to keep the full routine.
games.why: Lawrence turned the cake in the pan for love of God. In a full season, prayer shrinks and moves into the work.

practice: Pick up something from your day: a mug, a spoon, a pen. Turn it over slowly, once, the way Lawrence turned the cake in the pan, and name your busy-season version: what your practice shrinks to on the fullest day.
For the rest of the sit, hold the object, and come back to its weight with each breath.

wordCard.voice: Busy seasons: the stretches when life is too full, when practice shrinks to fit inside the work, the way Brother Lawrence prayed at the stove.

carryVoice: Your line: smaller, not stopped. A flip of the pan can be a prayer. Day 1670, done in the middle of things.
